---
title: "The Oracle Never Says Yes"
abstract: |
  Philosophers who ask "What is knowledge?" test proposed analyses against cases, and the test is lopsided: a case can refute an analysis, and nothing the cases do ever confirms one. I model this as learning from counterexamples only and show that the number of refutations an analyst must expect is fixed by the vocabulary of case-features the analysis is allowed to use, not by the skill of the cases offered. It equals, up to a logarithmic factor, the size of the largest minimal set of case verdicts that no analysis in the vocabulary can jointly respect. The same number is the size of the certificate that shows the vocabulary to be wrong. Two consequences follow. A long run of patches to a definition is what a rich, unconstrained vocabulary predicts, so the run is not evidence that the patching is hopeless or that a fourth condition is waiting; and the price of demanding a definition, as opposed to a mere predictor of verdicts, can be exponential. The method of cases can drive a debate to convergence but cannot certify that it has converged, and what tells an analyst to stop is a restriction on the vocabulary that no case supplies.
bibliography: oracle-never-says-yes.bib

## The asymmetry {#sec-asym}

When philosophers ask what knowledge is, they propose an analysis, and others reply with a case. The case is either a counterexample or it is not. In the history of this practice, nobody has returned a case that shows an analysis to be correct. Cases of agreement are cheap and carry no weight: that the proposed conditions are satisfied in every ordinary instance of knowledge is the reason the analysis was proposed. Whatever else the method of cases is, it is a source of one-sided feedback. The analyst learns "no, not that, here is a case" or learns nothing.

The practice has also gone on for a very long time. After @Gettier1963 the analyses of knowledge multiplied and so did the counterexamples, and the sequence has the shape of an arms race that neither side wins. The standard responses are two. One says that the sequence shows the analysis to be impossible, because knowledge is unanalysable [@Williamson2000]. The other says that the right fourth condition has not yet been found. Both treat the length of the sequence as evidence about the target. I think the length is first of all evidence about the question, specifically about the class of analyses that were allowed to be tried, and that this is a question with a precise answer.

The question is: how many counterexamples should an analyst expect to need, as a function of what kinds of analyses she permits herself? The relevant mathematics exists. @Angluin1988 studied learning from equivalence queries, in which a learner proposes a hypothesis and a teacher either accepts or returns a counterexample. @Littlestone1988 studied the equivalent mistake-bound model. A learner who must answer from counterexamples alone is in exactly the position of an analyst facing the method of cases, with one difference that I take to be the point. In those models the teacher eventually says "yes". Here she does not. I will argue that this one change leaves the count of refutations as the learning theorists computed it, and removes the thing the learning theorists took for granted, which is the signal to stop.

The contribution is not the formula; it is what the formula says about an old philosophical practice. In @sec-model I set out the model and the quantity that governs it. In @sec-gettier I apply it to Gettier-patching, and in @sec-price I draw out the price of demanding definitions. In @sec-stop I argue that termination needs a restriction on the vocabulary that cases cannot validate. @sec-objections takes the objections I think matter most, and @sec-prior says what is already known.

## Cases, vocabularies and refutations {#sec-model}

Let a *case* be an item described by a vector of $n$ binary features, drawn from a stock of possible features that I will call the *vocabulary*. Let the target be a verdict function that assigns each case "F" or "not F". An *analysis* in the vocabulary is a function from feature vectors to verdicts; a *class* $C$ is the set of analyses the analyst is prepared to consider. The oracle knows the target. At each stage the analyst puts forward an analysis $h$; the oracle returns a case on which $h$ and the target disagree, or declares nothing if there is none, and the analyst then stops, because she cannot tell the difference between "nothing" and "nothing yet". I count the refutations the analyst endures before her proposal agrees with the target everywhere. Call this the *refutation count*.

Three features of the setup are idealisations that I keep for now and revisit in @sec-objections: verdicts are noise-free; cases are describable in the vocabulary; and a target exists. The model is not offered as a description of philosophical practice at the level of detail. It is offered as a model of what the asymmetry alone guarantees, so that what the asymmetry alone guarantees can be separated from what is specific to knowledge.

**Worst case.** If the oracle may choose which counterexample to return, the analyst's minimax count depends on the class and on a restriction I come to in a moment. A conjunctive vocabulary is the easy case. Suppose the target is a conjunction of some of $n$ features, and the analyst starts with the conjunction of all of them and drops any feature that a counterexample shows to be unnecessary. Then every refutation removes at least one wrongly included condition, and at most $n$ refutations occur. The adversary can force all $n$: it returns, each time, a case that has every feature but one superfluous one. At the opposite extreme, if the class is all Boolean functions of the $n$ features, an adversary can return a different case each time, and each refutation corrects only the one case it concerns, so $2^{n}$ cases are needed and the count is exponential in $n$. I verified these by exhaustive computation on small classes and by simulation up to $n=1024$ (supplementary code, `exact_tables.py` and `sim_oracles.py`); the point is not that they are surprising but that the same oracle, equally skilled, yields linear and exponential counts depending only on what the analyst was willing to propose.

**Proper and improper hypotheses.** Here a distinction matters that philosophy has not marked. A *proper* analysis is a member of the class: a definition, a set of conditions stated in the vocabulary. An *improper* hypothesis is any verdict-predictor at all, including one assembled case by case from what has been learned so far. @Angluin1988 distinguishes the two cases; @Littlestone1988 shows that for the improper case the worst-case count is exactly a combinatorial quantity of the class, now called its Littlestone dimension, $\mathrm{Ldim}(C)$. The class of single-feature analyses, "F if and only if feature $i$", for instance, has Littlestone dimension about $\log_2 n$: a predictor that takes a majority vote among the single-feature analyses still consistent with the cases seen halves its candidates with every mistake. A proper analyst who must name one feature at a time, however, can be refuted $n-1$ times: the adversary returns, each time, a case on which only the named feature is superfluous. In my simulations the numbers are 1023 versus 10 at $n=1024$, while random counterexamples give about 8. The gap is not an artefact. A hypothesis that has to be a definition forgoes the majority vote.

**What governs the proper count.** Let a set of labelled cases be *inconsistent* for $C$ if no analysis in $C$ gives all of them the stated verdicts, and *minimal* if every proper subset is consistent. Let $K^{*}(C)$ be the size of the largest minimal inconsistent set. For single-feature analyses $K^{*}=n$: take cases $x_1,\dots,x_n$, where $x_i$ has feature $i$ alone, each with verdict "not F"; every single-feature analysis is violated by one of them, but dropping $x_j$ leaves feature $j$ respecting the rest, so the set is minimal. The general fact, proved by @Hanneke2021 in a closely related form, is that the proper count is at least $\max\{\mathrm{Ldim}(C),\,K^{*}(C)-1\}$, and at most the product of $\mathrm{Ldim}(C)$, $K^{*}(C)$ and a logarithm of $K^{*}(C)$. I checked the lower bound by computing exact minimax values on 145 random small classes together with the named classes; it held in all of them, and the product bound was never violated (output in `exact_results.txt`). The reading I want to put on this is not in the learning-theory literature that I have found. $K^{*}$ is the size of the biggest body of case verdicts that is *jointly* intolerable to every analysis in the vocabulary, although every part of it is tolerable. It measures how far the vocabulary is from being able to represent whatever the cases happen to say.

**$K^{*}$ is also the certificate.** Two cases that agree on every feature in the vocabulary and differ in verdict, a *twin pair*, refute every analysis in the vocabulary at once. $K^{*}$ plays an analogous role for a vocabulary that is wrong in a less brutal way: a minimal inconsistent set of size $k$ is a body of $k$ verdicts which shows, once it is assembled, that no analysis in the class is right, and any proof that the class is wrong needs at least a set of that kind. So the number that tells the analyst how many refutations she must be ready to bear is the number that tells her how many cases she must hold in view to see that her vocabulary is the problem. That connection is the thing I use below. It is a way of putting the Duhem-Quine point quantitatively: a single case cannot indict a class, it indicts a particular analysis; a class is indicted by a set, and the size of the set is $K^{*}$.

## Gettier patching as the expected behaviour {#sec-gettier}

Suppose the analyst begins with justified true belief and the vocabulary is the one @Gettier1963 and his early readers had: features of the subject's evidence, of her belief, of the proposition's truth and of the relation between them. Consider what the method predicts and what it does not.

*It predicts a run of refutations.* The class of analyses the early tradition was prepared to entertain is the class of conjunctions of conditions on features of this kind, with some disjunctions, which is large and contains many interlocking conditions. Against such a class the adversarial count is large, and even an indifferent sequence of counterexamples will exceed a handful of refutations. The first is cheap and the later ones are not. The long run of cases that followed Gettier is therefore not a surprise on this model.

*It predicts patching.* An elimination procedure, which is what the proper analyst with a conjunctive vocabulary is, responds to each counterexample by adding or modifying a condition so as to exclude it. Each modification, being minimal, is about as small a change as the vocabulary permits. This is how defeasibility, no-false-lemma, causal and reliabilist amendments look when read as moves in the model: each is chosen so as to preserve verdicts on the cases already seen. The model predicts, in other words, that the sequence will consist of local repairs and not of large changes, because local repair is the only strategy that preserves what has been secured.

*It predicts the recipe.* @Zagzebski1994 argues that any analysis on which justification does not entail truth is open to the construction of Gettier cases, by taking a case of justified false belief and adding a lucky coincidence that makes the belief true. This is, in the model's terms, a strategy for the oracle that works against a whole family of analyses at once. A strategy of this kind is not a single counterexample; it is a way of generating counterexamples to every member of a class that satisfy a stated schema. What it shows is a feature of the *class*: that no analysis in it, however modified, escapes. A dispute about whether the recipe works is a dispute about whether this is a legitimate class-level refutation, and the model gives the dispute its proper shape. The standard objection is that the recipe's cases are not clearly cases of non-knowledge; I come to this in @sec-objections.

*It does not predict that there is a fourth condition.* The tradition has often treated the repeated failure as a sign that the right extra condition had not yet been found. On the model, how long the run is tells us nothing about whether such a condition exists, because the long run would be seen whether it exists or not. If the target is a conjunction of a few features in the vocabulary, the elimination analyst reaches it in a few steps; if the target is not in the class, she is refuted without end. The record of refutations is the same up to a point in the two cases, and the point is exactly where the cases stop being informative: the observation that cases keep arriving is not evidence for either hypothesis.

*It does not predict that the target is unanalysable.* @Williamson2000 infers from the failure of analyses that knowledge is unanalysable, with the concept of knowledge primitive. The model gives no support to that inference as such, for the same reason. But it supports a different one, which is that if the target is simple enough to be in the class, then the cases should eventually converge, and that the lack of convergence over a very long time is evidence that the class is wrong. That is evidence of a different kind from Williamson's: evidence that the *vocabulary* does not suffice, which can be remedied without giving up on analysis, but not by adding conditions. @Weatherson2003 makes a related point, from the opposite side: that counterexamples to analyses can be overweighted against a background of naturalness, so that what we should want is the simplest analysis that fits most of the cases and not every one. In the model's terms this is a restriction on the class, and the next sections argue that it is the only thing that can end the run.

I have so far used "the vocabulary" as if it were given. It is not, and any application of the model to the actual debate requires a decision about which features a case is described in terms of. I have not tried to replay the Gettier literature by encoding the analyses as feature vectors, because any such encoding would be my own invention and the numbers it produced would be an artefact of the encoding; whatever the model says about the literature, it says as a prediction of shape and not of number.

## The price of demanding a definition {#sec-price}

The contrast between proper and improper hypotheses has a philosophical reading. To demand a *definition* is to demand a proper hypothesis. To be content with a *predictor* of verdicts, a procedure that says for any case whether the target applies, is to permit an improper one. For single-feature vocabularies the difference between 1023 and 10 refutations is already striking. For richer classes it can be the difference between a number that is finite and one that is not. Some classes, those of unbounded Littlestone dimension, defeat every learner whatever its form, and the model has nothing to say about those beyond what it says about the case of a target outside the vocabulary. But there are classes of finite Littlestone dimension for which the proper count is unbounded, and in such classes the analyst who insists on defining is refuted without end while the analyst who is content to predict is refuted only a bounded number of times. The learning-theoretic result I rely on is due to @Hanneke2021. I have not found its philosophical significance remarked on, though my search was limited (see @sec-prior).

The philosophical moral is not that definitions are bad. It is that there is a price for the form, and that the price is quantifiable and may be large. The tradition's own practice supports this. The community that produces and discusses the analyses is not one proper analyst; it is an ensemble, and the way it answers a new case in the seminar room is not by reciting one definition but by consulting the several definitions and the intuitions about the case, which looks very much like a vote among surviving candidates. A community of rival analyses, each of which is refuted in turn, is the pattern of a majority-vote predictor, and the model says that it is a cheap way to proceed. It is cheaper than any one of its members could have been, and the reason is that the community does not require any one definition to be right. The cost of this arrangement is that nothing in the arrangement is a definition. What the community has, at any time, is a predictor of verdicts with a record of how often it has been wrong, not an answer to "What is F?".

There is a second contrast, which concerns the source of the cases. The standard picture has the analyst proposing and the critic supplying counterexamples. A different picture has the analyst probing: asking, for a case already in hand, what happens to the verdict if one feature is changed. The Socratic elenchus, as Vlastos describes it, has the first shape: the interlocutor proposes, Socrates refutes [@Vlastos1982]. The Meno problem, how one could ever recognise a correct answer to "What is virtue?" if one did not already know it [@PlatoMeno], is on this model the observation that the refuting oracle can never certify. Plato's dialogues of definition end in aporia more often than not, the *Theaetetus* among them [@PlatoTheaetetus], and the model suggests that this is what a refutation-only exchange with a rich class should produce. Self-posed probes do better against some classes, and I have checked that a one-feature-at-a-time probe finds the relevant features of a conjunction in $n$ queries (`probes.py`, which also shows the masking failure), but it fails when the target has two ways of being satisfied, because a change to one feature is masked by the other; this is the old problem of the plurality of causes that Mill's method of difference was known to face [@Mill1843]. Probing is not a way out. It is an additional source of information with its own failure condition.

## Stopping {#sec-stop}

The title says that the oracle never says yes. Termination in the ordinary models is the oracle's saying so, and the philosophical method lacks it. What could take its place? There are three candidates.

*Exhaustion.* The analyst might wait until the cases run out. But cases are not a finite store; for a rich class there are exponentially many, and the analyst cannot know that the ones she has been given are all the ones there are.

*Certification by the cases themselves.* If cases could tell us that the analyst has converged, the method would be a source of confirmation, and it is not.

*A restriction on the class.* The remaining candidate is that the analyst commits to a class small enough that a bounded number of refutations settles the question: a conjunctive vocabulary of few conditions, say, for which $K^{*}$ is small and the elimination analyst is within $n$ refutations of being right if the target is in the class at all. Then the analyst has a stopping rule that she can state in advance: if more than $n$ refutations have occurred, the target is not in the class. The rule is a *tripwire*. It does not say when the analyst is right; it says when she is wrong about the class. In the language of formal learning theory, the class is refutable relative to the cases, in the sense of @Kelly1996: a wrong class will be exposed in a bounded number of refutations, but a right one is never certified as right [@Kelly1996; @Kelly1997]. The point is that the stopping rule comes from the restriction on the class, which is a commitment prior to the cases; no case can supply it.

This is the point at which the model meets the older problem of simplicity. The restriction that makes a tripwire available is a simplicity restriction. Why should the analyst prefer a small class? The usual answers say that simple theories are more likely to be true. @Kelly2007 argues that a preference for simplicity can be justified without any claim that simplicity indicates truth: a method that always conjectures the simplest theory compatible with the data has fewest retractions, in the worst case, among methods that converge to the truth. On the model here that is the right kind of justification. The analyst who starts with the small class and enlarges it only when forced to do so by a refutation-set of the right kind, as I have described, changes her mind as seldom as the problem allows. She has not been told, by anything, that the small class is true. What she has is a rule of procedure and a guarantee about the number of revisions.

I take this to be the content of the idea, found in @Weatherson2003 and in much of the reception of @Gettier1963, that the response to Gettier is to give up a requirement that an analysis fit every case. It is not that the cases are fallible, though they may be. It is that the only thing that licenses an analyst to stop is a restriction on what she will consider, and cases do not supply restrictions. This accounts for the fact that the practice has not stopped. It also accounts for the fact that the practice has sometimes seemed to stop, as it does in cases like "bachelor": if the vocabulary in which we state the analysis is small, a handful of cases suffices to bring the elimination analyst to the right answer, and her proposal is not refuted afterwards, so that the community gradually stops asking. Nothing certifies that she has arrived. The absence of refutation, over a long time, in a small class, is as close as the method gets to a yes.

A prediction follows that can be wrong. If this is right, then the question of how many refutations a debate will take is answered by the size of the minimal inconsistent sets that its vocabulary admits, and debates over analyses in rich vocabularies, those in which the proposals are not bounded in complexity, should show runs of refutation far longer than debates in which the vocabulary is tight, and should not settle by refutation. The tradition's experience with knowledge, causation, personal identity and free action looks like the first kind, and with *bachelor*, *triangle* and *grandmother* like the second. This is a qualitative claim, I have not measured it, and it is cheap enough that someone with the historical record could check it. If the long-running debates turn out to differ from the quickly settled ones in some other way, such as in how contested the target's application is, the prediction fails.

## Objections {#sec-objections}

**"Cases are not discrete features."** Williamson's view is that the concept of knowledge is not a structure of conditions, and prototype views hold that application is graded by similarity to exemplars. The model has an answer to the first and a weaker one to the second. If features are binary and the verdict is a function of them, the model applies. If the verdict depends on similarity to a prototype, then the class of similarity-based analyses is itself a class in a vocabulary of exemplars; the model applies to that vocabulary, with the same result for the refutation count. What the model cannot do is tell us which vocabulary we are in. That is the objection's force: the quantitative results are relative to a vocabulary, and a choice of vocabulary is a choice of $K^{*}$. I accept this. It is why the results are stated as relative to a class, and why the one result that is not relative, the absence of certification, is the one I have put at the centre.

**"Intuitions about cases are noisy."** Experimental work finds that verdicts in Gettier cases vary across people and framings [@Weinberg2001; @Turri2015]. Noise changes the model in a way that matters. A counterexample with a noisy verdict is a counterexample with some probability, and a refutation that is not reliable cannot force a revision. Two things follow. The worst-case count is overstated, because the adversary cannot rely on any particular case. But the stopping problem is worse, because a long absence of refutations is now also compatible with an oracle that is merely unreliable about the cases that matter. The remedy that the learning theorists adopted when the teacher was not available, replacing equivalence queries by random examples and requiring approximate correctness [@Angluin1988], gives up the quantifier over cases that philosophers care about. The analyst would then say "right except on a small proportion of cases", and *knowledge* is a concept whose philosophical interest lies in the strange cases, not the proportion.

**"Some refutations are bad."** The recipe in @sec-gettier assumes that the cases it generates are cases of non-knowledge. If a recipe's cases are disputed, the recipe is a disputed adversary, and the model applies to the dispute with the disputed cases removed from the oracle's repertoire. It will then take fewer refutations to reach convergence, and the class may no longer be refuted. This is a real gap in what the model delivers. A model of refutation cannot adjudicate which refutations count, and the debates that matter, such as the one about whether @Zagzebski1994's cases are knowledge-denying, are of this kind. What the model supplies is a precise statement of what is at stake in them: a class-level refutation holds or fails depending on whether a stated schema of cases is admitted into the oracle's repertoire.

**"The model fits; that does not show it explains."** The worry is that I have chosen a model that reproduces a long run and called the run explained. There are two replies. The first is that the model makes one prediction, in @sec-stop, that is not a retrodiction and could fail. The second is that the contribution I claim is not the match of a model to the history but the separation of two things the history fuses: what is attributable to the asymmetry of the method, which is the count's dependence on the vocabulary and the absence of a stopping signal, and what is attributable to the target. A model that makes the first separable from the second is explanatory in the sense that matters here even if it does not predict the sequence of proposals.

**"There may be no target."** If "knowledge" is a cluster concept, or if usage does not determine a function, then there is no target function and the count is not defined. In that case the refutation sequence is unbounded for a reason that has nothing to do with the class. The model does not distinguish this from the case of a target outside the vocabulary, since the oracle is indistinguishable from the analyst's side. This is a consequence and not an escape: a debate that never converges does not by that fact tell us whether the target lacks a definition or lacks a definition in this vocabulary, and that is just what the model predicts about how little the run of cases can tell us. @Chalmers2015 holds that philosophy makes progress in the form of negative results, elimination of options, and not in the form of convergence on answers. The model lends that view a structural basis. A refutation-only method accumulates eliminations, and the number of eliminations it can accumulate is bounded by the vocabulary, not by the philosophers' effort.

**"Reply to an existing literature."** The model uses results from learning theory, and I have applied them to a debate in the philosophy of knowledge. I take the debate to be an instance and the topic to be the structure of inquiry by cases, which is a problem philosophers have faced since the *Meno*.

## What is known already {#sec-prior}

The central results are not mine. The proper/improper distinction and the equivalence-query model are @Angluin1988; the mistake-bound model, the dimension and its role in the improper case are @Littlestone1988; the proper-learning bounds that I use in terms of the dual Helly number are @Hanneke2021. Language identification in the limit and the idea that learning without negative evidence is impossible for rich classes are @Gold1967; the philosophical development of the learning-theoretic view of inquiry, including verifiability and refutability relative to a hypothesis set and the justification of simplicity by efficiency, is Kelly's [@Kelly1996; @Kelly2007]. Within philosophy, the closest antecedent that I have found for applying a learning-from-queries model to the analysis of concepts is the discussion of the *Meno* as a learning problem by Glymour and Kelly, which I know only in outline and have not been able to read in full. The inference that cases can only refute and the diagnosis of Gettier cases as class-level are due to the literature on Gettier, which I have read in selection.

What I add is narrow, and I state it so. First, a reading of the quantity that governs the proper count as the largest minimal set of verdicts that no analysis in a vocabulary can respect, which is also the size of the smallest body of cases that could show the vocabulary to be wrong. Second, the application of the proper/improper contrast to the philosophical demand for a definition and to the community of analysts as an ensemble. Third, the diagnosis of what in the Gettier sequence is expected under the asymmetry and what is not, with the consequence that the length of the sequence is no evidence about whether a fourth condition exists. Fourth, the thesis that a stopping rule must come from a restriction on the class, supplied before the cases, and the claim that this is where simplicity enters the practice of analysis. None of the four is a new theorem. Whether the four together are an advance on what has been said about Gettier and the paradox of analysis [@Shope1983] is for the reader to judge; I have not found them stated together.

## Conclusion

The oracle never says yes. The cost of working without that signal is set before the first case is offered, by what the analyst is willing to propose, and the sign that she should stop is not something the cases can give. If the method of cases is to be trusted to end an inquiry, what ends it must be the analyst's choice of a small enough class, made in advance and kept to, together with a count she has promised to take as the sign that she chose wrongly.
